intro: An ambush prayer in eighteen verses. The heading sets it on the night Saul posted men around David's house, and the psalm keeps that setting all the way through: enemies who work after dark, a speaker waiting for morning. It runs in two panels, each closed by Selah at {{6.15}} and {{14.11}}, and each panel carries the same two refrains, the enemies who come back at evening and growl like a dog, and God who is a high fortress. One thing to watch for a learner: the root of {{2.4}}, to set someone up out of reach, is the same root as the noun in {{10.5}}, so the verb of the opening plea and the noun of the closing refrain are the same idea in two shapes. Note also that Hebrew counts the heading as verse 1, so every verse number here is one ahead of most English Bibles.

stichs.en: For the leader; to Do Not Destroy. Of David, a michtam.
When Saul sent men, and they watched the house to kill him.

verses.summary: The heading does two jobs at once: it names a melody and it names a night. Everything after it is read through a house under surveillance.

stichs.en: Rescue me from my enemies, my God;
from those who rise against me, set me up out of reach.

glosses: from those who rise against me
set me high out of reach
verses.summary: Two verbs with the object suffix -ni, me, and both are verbs of removal rather than of victory. The request is height, not conquest.

stichs.en: Rescue me from those who do harm,
and from men of bloodshed save me.

verses.summary: The same opening verb repeats, and the enemies get named twice over, first by what they do and then by what they are made of.

stichs.en: For look, they lie in wait for my life;
fierce men gather against me,
for no offence of mine and no sin of mine, LORD.

verses.summary: The plea acquires its argument here. The speaker is not asking to be forgiven, he is asking to be believed: nothing he did started this.

stichs.en: For no guilt of mine they run and take up position.
Wake up, come to meet me, and look.

verses.summary: Three imperatives thrown at God in a row. The enemies are already moving and the psalm treats divine sleep as the immediate problem.

stichs.en: And You, LORD God of hosts, God of Israel,
rouse Yourself to call every nation to account;
show no mercy to any of these treacherous wrongdoers. Selah.

verses.summary: The longest verse in the psalm, and the widest. A private ambush is suddenly argued at the scale of all the nations, which is what makes this psalm usable by anyone who is not David.

stichs.en: They come back at evening,
they growl like a dog,
and circle the city.

verses.summary: The refrain. Not a battle line but a patrol: they arrive on a schedule, they make noise, they go round again.

stichs.en: Look, they pour it out with their mouth,
swords are in their lips:
for who is listening?

verses.summary: The weapon in this psalm is speech, and the last three words are the enemies quoted directly. Their whole confidence rests on an assumption about an empty sky.

stichs.en: But You, LORD, laugh at them;
You mock all the nations.

verses.summary: The answer to who is listening, placed immediately after the question and using the same opening words as verse 6. Someone is listening, and the reply is laughter rather than rescue.

stichs.en: His strength: for You I keep watch,
for God is my high fortress.

verses.summary: The watchers outside the house are answered by a watcher inside it, and the verb is the same one used of them in the heading. The first word is a known textual crux, discussed below.

stichs.en: The God of loyalty to me will come out to meet me;
God will let me look on those who watch for my fall.

verses.summary: The verb of meeting is the one used for arriving ahead of time. God is imagined getting there before the ambush does.

stichs.en: Do not kill them, or my people will forget;
make them stagger by Your power and bring them down, our shield, my Lord.

verses.summary: The strangest request in the psalm and its moral centre. A dead enemy teaches nothing, so the prayer asks for a defeat that stays visible.

stichs.en: The sin of their mouth, the word of their lips:
let them be caught in their own pride,
and for the cursing and lying they keep telling.

verses.summary: The punishment is derived from the offence rather than added to it: mouths that made swords are to be caught by what came out of them.

stichs.en: Finish them in fury, finish them, and let them be gone,
and let people know that God rules in Jacob,
to the ends of the earth. Selah.

glosses: and let them be no more
verses.summary: This sits awkwardly against verse 12, which asked that they not be killed. The tension is in the text and the psalm does not resolve it; what both verses share is that the point is what gets known afterwards.

stichs.en: And they come back at evening,
they growl like a dog,
and circle the city.

verses.summary: The refrain returns word for word except for one added conjunction at the front. Nothing outside has changed yet, which is the point of repeating it.

stichs.en: They roam about for food,
and if they are not full they stay out all night.

verses.summary: The dog image is carried one step further than the refrain does, into scavenging. The verb of roaming is the one the speaker asked for in verse 12, so the prayer is being answered in the enemies' own behaviour.

stichs.en: But as for me, I will sing of Your strength,
and at morning I will sing out Your loyalty,
for You have been a high fortress to me,
and a place to run on the day I was in trouble.

verses.summary: The one verse that steps outside the night. Everything the enemies do happens at evening; the single word {{17.4}} is the whole answer to them.

stichs.en: My strength, to You I will make music,
for God is my high fortress, the God of loyalty to me.

verses.summary: The refrain of verse 10 comes back with the phrase from verse 11 attached to it, so the ending gathers the two halves of the psalm into one line.

pardes.body: Two panels of roughly equal size, each ending in Selah. Panel one runs to verse 6 and is mostly petition; panel two runs to verse 14 and is mostly sentence. Each panel is followed by the same two-part refrain, the enemies at evening in verses 7 and 15, and God as a high fortress in verses 10 and 18. Read the refrains next to each other and the psalm's shape is obvious: the situation outside the house does not change between them, and the speaker does. What is asked for is never the destruction of the siege but relocation above it, which is why the vocabulary of height carries the argument from {{2.4}} at the start to {{18.5}} at the end.

The crux is the first word of verse 10, {{10.0}}, which the Masoretic text vocalises as his strength while the matching line at {{18.0}} has my strength. The two verses are otherwise a pair, so many translations read the first as my strength too and treat the difference as a copying slip; others keep it and take it as a reference to the enemy's strength, which the speaker answers by watching for God. The reading is disputed and both are defensible from the consonants. Second thing to notice: the noun in {{10.5}} and the verb in {{2.4}} share a root meaning to be too high to reach, so a fortress in this psalm is not a wall you hide behind but an elevation. Third, the fierce ones of {{4.6}} is a word for insolence and force together, and it is the same adjective used of a strong animal, which sets up the dog of {{7.3}} before the dog arrives.

Verse 12 has drawn the most attention: do not kill them, so that my people will not forget. The line has long been read as asking for a living monument rather than a clean victory, on the reasoning that a defeated enemy still walking around teaches the lesson that a buried one cannot. Read this way the psalm asks for something harder than rescue, namely a permanent visible reminder, and the tension with verse 14, which asks that they be finished off, is left standing rather than smoothed away. The heading points to the night in the book of Samuel when Saul's men surrounded the house, and the dogs of verses 7 and 15 have often been taken as those watchers rather than as animals, which turns the refrain into a description of a specific stakeout instead of a general image of menace.

The psalm is organised on an axis of evening against morning. The enemies belong entirely to the night: they return at evening in verses 7 and 15, they roam to eat and lodge out until dawn in verse 16, and their weapon is speech spoken in the dark on the assumption that no one hears. The speaker owns exactly one time of day, the {{17.4}} of verse 17, and what he sings there is loyalty. In the mystical reading the night is the state of concealment in which judgment operates unopposed and the morning is the return of loyal love, so the psalm is not asking for the night to be shortened but for the singer to be held above it until it turns. The high fortress is then a description of consciousness, not of masonry: the same house, the same watchers outside it, and a person who has been raised out of their reach without being moved.
